title: Bitcoin: A Peer-to-Peer Electronic Cash System
subject: Cryptocurrency
summary: Proposes digital money that people can send directly to each other, with no bank in the middle, using a shared chain of proof-of-work.

intro.title: A New Quest
intro.speaker: PROF. QUANT
pages: Welcome, scholar! Today's paper: "Bitcoin: A Peer-to-Peer Electronic Cash System".
It is 9 pages long. I turned it into 4 worlds: Digital Cash Quest, The Proof-of-Work Mines, The Disk Diet, The Masked Ledger.
An AI helped me explain this paper in plain words. AI can slip up, so check anything important against the paper.
Move with A and D, jump with W. Stomp bears for fun facts, and reach each flag for a lesson. Go!

worlds.name: World 1: Digital Cash Quest

cutscenes.title: The Trouble With Trust
cutscenes.speaker: PROF. QUANT
pages: Welcome, friends! I'm Prof. Quant. Today we look at why buying stuff online is a bit clunky.
Right now, we rely on banks and credit card companies to handle every single web payment.
Because middlemen step in to settle fights, you can never have a truly final, non-reversible deal.
Merchants must ask for extra personal info just to stay safe, baking fraud right into the system!

practice.prompt: Why do online merchants have to ask customers for extra personal details in a traditional bank-based system?
choices: Because payments can be reversed
To speed up shipping times
To open a physical bank branch
To pay state sales tax
practice.explanation: Since banks can reverse payments, merchants face fraud risks and must collect extra info to protect themselves.

cutscenes.title: Coins and Cheaters
cutscenes.speaker: PROF. QUANT
pages: What if a coin was just a digital chain of signatures, passing ownership from one person to the next?
You can check the math to see who owned the coin last. Neat, right?
Ah, but here's the catch! How do you know the seller didn't spend the exact same coin twice somewhere else?
Usually, a central mint checks every single transaction to stop this sneaky trick known as double-spending.

practice.prompt: What is the main danger when a payee receives a digital coin directly from a previous owner?
choices: Internet connection might drop
The owner might double-spend it
The file size might be too large
The digital signature will expire
practice.explanation: Without a central check, a dishonest owner could try to spend the same digital coin with two different people.

cutscenes.title: Time Stamping Magic
cutscenes.speaker: PROF. QUANT
pages: To ditch the central mint, everyone needs to agree on which transaction happened first.
Meet the timestamp server! It takes a batch of data, scrambles it into a unique code called a hash, and publishes it.
Each new timestamp links to the previous one, locking the exact order of events into an unbreakable chain.
As long as honest folks control the majority of computer power, we can prove what happened without any boss!

practice.prompt: How does a timestamp server prove that a piece of data existed at a specific moment in time?
choices: By hashing it and publishing the code
By emailing a receipt to a bank
By printing it in a phone book
By notarizing it with a lawyer
practice.explanation: It takes the data, creates a hash, and publishes it widely so everyone can see it was locked in at that time.

facts: Online commerce relies almost entirely on trusted third-party financial institutions to process payments.
Completely non-reversible internet transactions are nearly impossible under traditional banking models.
An electronic coin is defined simply as a chain of digital signatures passed from owner to owner.
A traditional mint checks every single transaction to ensure no coin gets spent twice.
A timestamp server links data hashes together, making each new timestamp reinforce all the ones before it.

questions.prompt: Why can't we have completely non-reversible web payments using standard financial institutions?
choices: Digital signatures always expire daily
Computers are not fast enough yet
Banks must mediate disputes and reverse deals
Banks charge too much interest
questions.explanation: Financial institutions must step in to settle arguments, which makes completely non-reversible transactions impossible.

questions.prompt: What traditional method is normally used to prevent someone from double-spending a digital coin?
choices: Locking computers in a secure vault
Requiring a signature from the police
Charging a 50 percent fee on transfers
A central authority or mint checking it
questions.explanation: A central mint normally checks every transaction and issues brand new coins to stop double-spending.

questions.prompt: What is the primary purpose of publishing a hash through a timestamp server?
choices: To hide user identities completely
To speed up computer processors
To prove data existed at a specific time
To generate free internet data
questions.explanation: Publishing the hash proves the data existed at that time because it had to be inside to get that exact code.

worlds.name: World 2: The Proof-of-Work Mines

cutscenes.title: The Digital Scavenger Hunt
cutscenes.speaker: PROF. QUANT
pages: To keep our records safe, we use a digital puzzle called Proof-of-Work.
Imagine a lock that only opens if you find a specific secret code by guessing millions of combinations.
This 'nonce' is a number you change over and over until the resulting hash starts with a bunch of zeros.
It takes a lot of computer power to find this, so it proves you did real work.

practice.prompt: Why does a computer need to do so much work to find the right nonce?
choices: To increase the internet speed
To make it hard to cheat
To encrypt the user's password
To prove it has enough memory
practice.explanation: Solving the puzzle is hard, but checking the answer is easy. This makes it impossible for attackers to fake the record quickly.

cutscenes.title: Choosing the Longest Path
cutscenes.speaker: PROF. QUANT
pages: Sometimes two different blocks are found at the same time, creating a split in the path.
Nodes, or the computers in our network, always follow the longest chain they see.
If a shorter path exists, it gets abandoned when a longer, more verified path appears.
The longest chain is the winner because it represents the most total computer effort spent.

practice.prompt: What happens if a node finds two different versions of the next block?
choices: It works on the first one received
It picks one at random
It deletes both blocks
It crashes immediately
practice.explanation: Nodes work on the first version they get but keep the other one in case it ends up becoming part of a longer chain later.

cutscenes.title: Mining for Rewards
cutscenes.speaker: PROF. QUANT
pages: Why would anyone spend money on computers to run this network?
The first transaction in every block creates brand new coins for the person who solved the puzzle.
This is like gold miners digging for treasure; it pays them for their hard work.
Over time, fees from transactions will replace these new coins as the main reward.

practice.prompt: How do miners get paid if there is no bank handing out money?
choices: They earn coins by solving blocks
They steal from other users
The government sends them checks
They charge monthly subscriptions
practice.explanation: The network automatically issues new coins to the miner who successfully solves the block, acting as an incentive to keep going.

facts: Mining is compared to gold miners spending resources to add new gold to the world's supply.
Changing a past block requires redoing the work for that block and every single one after it.
A node can leave the network and rejoin later, just by looking for the longest chain.
If you pay a fee on a transaction, that extra amount goes to the miner as a reward.
An attacker's odds of overtaking the honest chain shrink very fast as the chain gets longer.

questions.prompt: Why can't an attacker easily change a transaction from three blocks ago?
choices: The hash is already deleted
They would need to redo all current work
They need a password from the bank
The network blocks their IP
questions.explanation: To change a past block, an attacker must redo the work for that block and every block added since, which is practically impossible.

questions.prompt: What ensures the network agrees on the truth?
choices: A pre-set list of rules
The longest chain of work
The fastest internet speed
A central voting committee
questions.explanation: The longest chain represents the majority of honest CPU power, making it the accepted source of truth.

questions.prompt: What is a nonce used for in this system?
choices: Calculating transaction fees
Encrypting private messages
Finding the required zero bits
Identifying the user's name
questions.explanation: Miners increment the nonce until the block's hash meets the difficulty requirement of having a specific number of leading zeros.

questions.prompt: How does the system prevent inflation forever?
choices: It burns coins randomly
It limits total computer power
It stops creating new coins eventually
It requires a central bank
questions.explanation: Once a set number of coins are out, the reward transitions to transaction fees only, keeping the system inflation-free.

questions.prompt: What happens if a node receives two branches of equal length?
choices: The network shuts down
It waits for a new block to break the tie
It rejects both branches
It asks the user to pick one
questions.explanation: The tie is broken as soon as the next proof-of-work is found, making one branch longer than the other.

worlds.name: World 3: The Disk Diet

cutscenes.title: Shrinking Old Blocks
cutscenes.speaker: PROF. QUANT
pages: Hey class! Prof. Quant here to help you save hard drive space.
Once a coin transaction is buried deep under new blocks, we don't need the old spent details anymore.
We can chop off those old branches in a process called compacting to save valuable space!

practice.prompt: When is it safe to discard old spent transaction details?
choices: Only when the computer restarts
Never, we must keep everything
Right after a single block is made
When buried under enough blocks
practice.explanation: Once a transaction is buried deep enough, old data can be tossed out to save disk space.

cutscenes.title: Lightweight Checking
cutscenes.speaker: PROF. QUANT
pages: Did you know a tiny block header is only about 80 bytes?
Because headers are so small, you can check payments without downloading the whole giant network node.
Businesses wanting extra speed and security might still run full nodes, though!

practice.prompt: How big is a typical block header without transactions?
choices: Zero bytes always
About 80 bytes
Exactly 80 megabytes
One whole gigabyte
practice.explanation: A stripped-down block header is roughly 80 bytes, making light checks super easy.

cutscenes.title: Splitting and Combining Coins
cutscenes.speaker: PROF. QUANT
pages: Making a separate transaction for every tiny cent would be super clumsy.
Instead, transactions use multiple inputs and outputs to easily split and combine value.
We never need a standalone history copy because complex branching is totally fine!

practice.prompt: How do transactions handle splitting and combining value?
choices: By deleting old coin histories
By making a transfer for every cent
Through a central bank approval
Using multiple inputs and outputs
practice.explanation: Transactions use multiple inputs and outputs so you don't need a separate transfer for every cent.

facts: Old transaction history can be safely deleted once buried under enough new blocks.
A block header with zero transactions is roughly 80 bytes tiny.
You do not need to run a full heavy network node just to verify payments.
Transactions use multiple inputs and outputs to easily split and combine money.
Complex transaction branching never requires extracting a complete standalone history.

questions.prompt: What happens to old spent transactions after they are buried under enough blocks?
choices: They are discarded to save disk space
They are locked forever in a vault
They are printed out on paper receipts
They are doubled in value automatically
questions.explanation: Buried transactions can be discarded to free up storage space.

questions.prompt: Roughly how large is a block header when all transactions are removed?
choices: 80 megabytes
80 bytes
80 kilobytes
80 gigabytes
questions.explanation: A block header without transactions weighs in at about 80 bytes.

questions.prompt: Why do transactions use multiple inputs and outputs?
choices: To split and combine value without separate cents transfers
To force everyone to run a full node
To confuse sneaky hackers on the network
To make the block headers bigger than 80 bytes
questions.explanation: Multiple inputs and outputs let you easily split and combine value without clumsy individual cent transfers.

questions.prompt: Who might still prefer running a full network node instead of a light check?
choices: Students taking a quick pop quiz
Businesses receiving frequent payments
Nobody, full nodes are totally illegal
Miners who only care about block headers
questions.explanation: Frequent payment businesses want independent security and quick verification.

questions.prompt: Is complex transaction branching (fan-out) a problem for this system?
choices: Yes, it requires 80 gigabytes per branch
No, it is handled fine without standalone history copies
Only if honest nodes lose control
Yes, it crashes the entire network instantly
questions.explanation: Fan-out is not a problem, and you never need a complete standalone history copy.

worlds.name: World 4: The Masked Ledger

cutscenes.title: Keeping Identities Secret
cutscenes.speaker: PROF. QUANT
pages: Welcome player! I'm Prof. Quant. Regular banks keep your info private by locking it away with a trusted company.
Our digital cash system does privacy differently. Everyone sees money moves, but names are hidden behind numbers.
To keep snoops from connecting your payments together, you must use a brand new cryptographic key pair for every single deal!

practice.prompt: Why should you use a brand new key pair for every transaction?
choices: To keep deals from linking to a common owner
To double the amount of coins you own
To make your computer run much faster
To unlock extra bonus levels
practice.explanation: Fresh key pairs act like firewalls, stopping snoops from linking your separate purchases to your real identity.

cutscenes.title: The Multi-Input Trap
cutscenes.speaker: PROF. QUANT
pages: Sometimes you need to combine a few past payments to make a bigger purchase. We call these multi-input transactions.
Even with secret keys, combining inputs leaves a tiny clue. It proves those funding sources belong to the exact same person.
If a snoop figures out just one of your keys, they might trace all your linked history. Privacy gets tricky here!

practice.prompt: What is the main privacy risk of multi-input transactions?
choices: They slow down the peer-to-peer network
They force you to use a traditional bank
They completely erase your digital coins
They reveal that their inputs share an owner
practice.explanation: Combining inputs leaks a connection, meaning if one key is cracked, related transactions might be exposed.

cutscenes.title: Beating the Secret Cheat
cutscenes.speaker: PROF. QUANT
pages: Imagine a sneaky player tries building a secret side-chain to double-spend coins they already handed over.
They can't invent free money or steal your funds, but they can try rewriting their own history in secret.
You stay safe by waiting for extra blocks to stack up. As more blocks pile on, the cheat's chance of winning drops to zero!

practice.prompt: What can a dishonest player achieve by building a secret side-chain?
choices: Shut down the entire peer-to-peer network
Steal coins belonging to completely random users
Try to take back money they recently spent
Create unlimited free money out of thin air
practice.explanation: Cheaters cannot create magic money or steal from others; they can only attempt to reverse their own recent payments.

facts: Traditional banks protect privacy by restricting information access to just the involved parties.
Using a fresh key pair for every transaction acts as a firewall against snoops.
Multi-input transactions inevitably reveal that their funding sources share an owner.
A dishonest sender trying to rewrite history is mathematically modeled as a Gambler's Ruin problem.
Waiting for z blocks to link after your payment causes the fraud probability to drop exponentially.

questions.prompt: What unavoidable event links transactions together even when using cryptography?
choices: Using multi-input transactions that share an owner
Waiting for z blocks to pile up on the chain
Sending coins to a financial institution
Leaving and rejoining the peer network
questions.explanation: Combining multiple inputs necessarily shows they were controlled by the same person, risking privacy if a key is exposed.

questions.prompt: Can a dishonest node secretly building an alternate chain create arbitrary money out of thin air?
choices: Yes, if they work fast enough in secret
Yes, because the network structure is minimal
No, honest nodes will reject invalid transactions
Only if they control all network CPU power
questions.explanation: The system rules stop arbitrary changes; honest nodes will never accept invalid blocks or fake money.

questions.prompt: What mathematical game describes an attacker trying to catch up to the honest chain from a deficit?
choices: An infinite loop of cryptographic hashing
A linear cryptographic key guessing race
A zero-sum digital poker tournament
A Binomial Random Walk and Gambler's Ruin
questions.explanation: The race between chains mirrors a Binomial Random Walk, and catching up is analogous to the Gambler's Ruin problem.
